<reason>Both sides argued the motion as written and clashed cleanly, but A built the sharper decisive structure and pressed it consistently. A's central dilemma — either "refuse" is worker-declared (and the hostile worker exploits it) or it is platform-adjudicated (and the motion is the appeals process renamed, run by the very gatekeeper PRO indicts for a decade of bad faith) — forced B into a mechanism concession, and A converted that concession into a live comparative: both remedies require compulsion, but code-level fixes (outlier discard, stripping rating rights from customers whose scores track names/accents) are auditable via published distributions, whereas a discretionary case-by-case "was the instrument measuring bias" review is unauditable and cheapest to deny. B's counter that a single adjudication is "auditable in court" was asserted but never developed into why that protects workers at scale better. A also handled B's best pressure question honestly and memorably (the star as low-friction tripwire that actually gets given and aggregates across unconnected raters; investigation is the response, not a substitute for the signal), and B's closing leaned on the "he conceded ratings can't be trusted to punish" turn without engaging that tripwire/response distinction — a recap gap at the exact place B claimed victory. B did well: the "your manager is the hostile customer holding a firing button" framing is vivid, the review-asks-a-different-question answer (instrument validity vs proportionality) genuinely blunted the "appeals renamed" charge, and equal dispatch/no badge answered the scarlet-letter question with a plausible analogy. But A's unanswered residue — after a granted opt-out the uneasy passenger's cheap safety signal goes nowhere, while high-friction complaint channels under-report exactly those incidents — plus a stray nonexistent reference id and slightly firmer unsourced framing on B's side, leave A with the cleaner reason to vote.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's rebuttal to the threshold-review answer: "You cannot indict the gatekeeper and then hand him the gate," paired with the auditability comparison (code change checkable by publishing rating distributions vs discretionary per-case review by the party incentivized to deny). It turned B's own bad-faith premise against B's mechanism, and B never resolved it.</best_rebuttal>
